title: Ang 885–916: Guru Arjan in Ramkali
hookLine: some say Ram, some Khuda, on ang 885
tomorrow: what does bliss sound like when it finally comes?

cards: Under almost any video about God, the comments fill up with names: God, Allah, Waheguru, Bhagwan, the Universe, and arguments over which one counts. Ang 885 has an odd detail.
It's a hymn by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, and its center line, the rahao, the pause, calls God Karim and Rahim: the Generous, the Merciful. Those are names from Arabic that Muslims use for God.
So what are they doing at the heart of a Sikh hymn?

teach.h: A LIST OF PEOPLE, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Read the whole hymn and the puzzle starts to solve itself. It's a list of people, side by side. In paraphrase: some say Ram, some Khuda.
Some serve Gusain, some Allah. Some bathe at holy rivers, some go on Hajj. Some do puja, some bow their heads to the ground.
Some read the Vedas, some the Kateb, the books of the prophets. Some wear blue, some white. Some call themselves Turk, some Hindu.
Some long for bhisht, some for svarg, two words for paradise. The Guru mocks no line. He doesn't say which side is right.
He sets them down like faces around one long table.
And in the middle, the pause: the Cause of all causes is Karim; shower your mercy, Rahim. The names the people use become the names in the prayer at the center.
In paraphrase: says Nanak, whoever recognizes the hukam, the divine order, knows the secret of the Master. Notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say names don't matter, or that all these practices are secretly one practice. People really do bathe in different rivers and read different books, and the hymn lets them stand.
What it asks lives underneath the name: do you see the order the One has set running?
The names are many. The secret is in the hukam.

how: Ragis sing Guru Arjan's Ramkali hymns in kirtan; the ang 885 hymn, with its pairs of Hindu and Muslim names and practices, is often explained in katha as a picture of the many ways people call on the One.

games.q: the pairs in the hymn — tap them.

s: the center line of the ang 885 hymn uses Arabic names for God
the rahao calls the One Karim, the Generous, and Rahim, the Merciful.
the hymn says all religions are the same
it lists real differences, rivers and Hajj, Vedas and Kateb, mocks none, and points to the hukam.
the hymn ends by naming the one right name for God
it ends on recognizing the hukam, the divine order, not on a name.

games.q: your little cousin hears a classmate call God Allah, and asks you: is that the same God or a different one? by the ang 885 hymn, what's your best answer?
o: people call the One by many names; the hymn says what matters is seeing the hukam.
it's all the same God, so every religion is really the same religion.
names don't matter at all, so it doesn't matter what anyone practices.
games.why: Guru Arjan sets Ram and Khuda, Gusain and Allah side by side, prays to Karim and Rahim, and ends on the hukam. he doesn't erase the differences; he points beneath them.

practice: Open to ang 885 if you can, and read the hymn's list out loud, slowly, one pair to a breath: Ram and Khuda, rivers and Hajj, Vedas and Kateb.
Then sit in the quiet after the last pair, the way the hymn ends on the hukam rather than on any one name.

wordCard.voice: Ang 885. Guru Arjan in Ramkali: some say Ram and some Khuda, and the pause at the center calls the One Karim and Rahim.

orig.note: Gurmukhi spelling of Karim, the Generous, a name of God from Arabic, in the rahao of the ang 885 hymn.

carryVoice: Many names: every one keeps its seat at the table, and the hymn points under them all to the hukam. Ang 885, read.
